head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: True once `strs[i]` is already strictly smaller than `strs[i+1]` in an earlier kept column, so later columns cannot hurt that pair
Lexicographic order is decided by the first differing column
Some still-tied pair would go out of order in column c
Detecting a column that must be deleted
Delete the column and leave `done` unchanged
A deleted column has no effect on the order
The kept column now separates this pair for good

p: The answer is `1`. Deleting column 0 leaves `a`, `b`, `c`, which is sorted.

bullets: Time: O(n * m) for n strings of length m.
Space: O(n) for `done`.

955.takeaway: Scan columns left to right; keep a column only if it does not break an adjacent pair that is still tied, and remember which pairs are already strictly ordered.

head: Code

Generating numbers with a no-leading-zero rule
The last digit of the number so far
A set of the two candidate digits; when k = 0 it has one element, so no duplicates

bullets: Time: O(2^n), since each number branches into at most 2 digits (about 9 * 2^(n-1) results at most).

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Only reverse steps while target is larger
Working from the goal back to the start
Reverse of "subtract 1" (halving is only possible on even numbers)
Once target <= start, only "subtract 1" forward steps are needed, so add the difference

p: Why backwards: going forward, doubling and subtracting do not combine greedily, but in reverse the choice is forced (even means halve, odd means add one).
Result: `1 + 5 - 4 = 2`, the moves 5 to 4 (subtract) to 8 (double). For `startValue = 2`, `target = 3`: 3 is odd so it becomes 4 (1 step), then 2 (2 steps), giving `2 + 2 - 2 = 2`.

bullets: Time: O(log target).
Space: O(1).

991.takeaway: Work backwards from the target: halve it when even, add 1 when odd, until it is not above the start; the remaining gap is closed by subtract-one steps.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: `*` binds tighter, so combine with the previous term
`/` combined with the previous term; for positive numbers truncation equals floor
`+` keeps x, `-` stores the negative, so the final sum handles both

bullets: Time: O(n).

1006.takeaway: Evaluate the expression with a stack: multiply and divide fold into the top of the stack immediately, while add and subtract push a signed number to be summed at the end.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Reads the dashes at the current position; their count is the node's depth
Parsing a depth encoded in text
The digits that follow the dashes are the node value
Reading a multi-digit number from a string
Climbs back up to the parent at depth - 1
Preorder visits the left child first, and a single child is always left, so fill left, then right
The node becomes the end of the current path
The first node ever pushed is the root and is never popped (depth 0 pops nothing before it)

bullets: Time: O(n) in the string length, each character is read once and each node popped at most once.
Space: O(h) for the stack, where h is the tree height.

1028.takeaway: Use a stack holding the current root-to-node path: the number of dashes is the depth, so pop until the stack length equals the depth and attach the new node to the top.

Knowing whether a character can still be placed later
Set of characters currently in the stack

Popping safely to get a smaller result

head: Code
Meaning

rows: Number of values in the sample
Needed for the mean and the median position
The values that occur, in increasing order; first and last are the minimum and maximum
Reading min and max from a histogram
Mean as the weighted sum divided by the count
The value with the highest count (unique by the statement)
The value at sorted position `pos` (0-indexed) found by accumulating counts until the running total passes `pos`
Order statistics without expanding the sample
Odd: the middle value; even: the average of the two middle values

bullets: Time: O(256), a constant (apart from the sum).
Space: O(256) for the list of present values, effectively O(1).

1093.takeaway: Work straight from the 256 counts: totals and mean by a sum, mode by the largest count, and the median by walking the cumulative counts to the middle position(s).

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: An opening bracket gets the label of its new depth's parity
A closing bracket gets the same label as its matching opener (it sits at the same depth)
Keeping each pair in one group

p: Why it works: each matching pair has one label, so both subsequences stay balanced, and consecutive depths alternate between the groups, so a depth of d becomes about d / 2 in each group.
Result `[0,1,1,1,1,0]`: group A is `()` and group B is `()()`, both with depth 1.

bullets: Time: O(n).
Space: O(n) for the output.

1111.takeaway: The parity of the nesting depth decides the group: parentheses at odd depth go to B and even depth to A, which splits the maximum depth in half.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Four sign choices for the `arr1` and `arr2` terms. The `i` sign is always +1, because swapping `i` and `j` gives the other sign
Replacing `|x| = max(x, -x)` by trying every sign
Value of index i under one sign choice
Splitting a pairwise expression into per-index values
The largest `value[i] - value[j]` over all pairs
The true answer is the maximum over the four choices

p: The answer is `13`, from indices 0 and 3: `3 + 7 + 3`.

bullets: Time: O(n), four passes.
Space: O(n) for the list of values.

1131.takeaway: Remove the absolute values by trying all sign combinations; each gives an expression s1*a + s2*b + i whose largest difference over all pairs is simply max - min.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Every ungrouped item becomes its own single-item group, so all items belong to a group
Kahn's algorithm: indegree counts, a heap of ready nodes, repeat; returns `None` if a cycle blocks some node
A dependency inside one group becomes an item edge; across groups it becomes a group edge
A valid order of the groups
Append each group's items in group order, so a group stays contiguous

p: Concatenated: `[6,3,4,5,2,0,1,7]`. If either level has a cycle, `topo` returns `None` and the answer is `[]`.

bullets: Time: O((n + e) log n) for n items and e dependencies, because of the heap.
Space: O(n + e).

1203.takeaway: Two layers of topological sort (Kahn's algorithm): first order the groups, then order the items inside each group, and concatenate.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: How high column j is already filled
Upper bound: unit squares only; a list so the inner function can change it
Prune: this branch cannot beat the best
Lowest level; if it equals the full height, the rectangle is tiled
Finding the next gap, and the finish test
The width of the lowest flat segment
A square must fit in this gap
Try the biggest square first, down to 1
Large pieces first finds good answers early, which prunes more
Place the square, recurse, then remove it

p: All columns reach height 2, so `best = 3`. Other branches (for example starting with a size-1 square) reach count 3 or more before finishing and are cut off or lose.

bullets: Time: exponential in the worst case; the pruning and the small limits (n, m at most 13) keep it fast.
Space: O(m) for `height` plus the recursion depth, which is at most the number of squares.

1240.takeaway: Backtracking on a skyline: always fill the lowest, leftmost gap with a square of some size, and prune any branch that already uses as many squares as the best answer.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Maximum (my score - opponent score) starting at stone i with me to move
`dp[n]` and the padding are 0: nothing left, no lead
Sum of the 1, 2 or 3 stones taken
My gain minus the opponent's best lead from the rest
The minimax recurrence as a difference
Positive lead means Alice wins, negative means Bob, zero is a tie

p: `dp[0] = -1 < 0`, so Alice (who moves first) ends behind: the answer is `"Bob"`.

bullets: Time: O(n), 3 options per position.
Space: O(n), reducible to O(1) with a rolling window.

1406.takeaway: `dp[i]` is the best score lead the player to move can get from stones i onward; taking 1 to 3 stones, the lead is what you take minus the opponent's best lead afterwards.
